theory.intro: The **circumference** is the distance around a circle. Rearranging $\pi = \frac{C}{d}$ gives $C = \pi d$, and because the diameter is double the radius, $C = 2\pi r$.
facts: $C = \pi d$ — use this when the **diameter** is given.
$C = 2\pi r$ — use this when the **radius** is given.
Use the calculator's $\pi$ key rather than $3.14$, and round only on the last line.
Leaving the answer as a multiple of $\pi$, such as $18\pi$ cm, is the **exact** circumference; a rounded decimal is written with $\approx$.
The circumference is a length, so its units match the units of the length given.
steps: Choose the formula that matches the length given.
Substitute the length into the formula.
Evaluate, then round as the question asks.

workedExamples.solution_text:
The marked length is the diameter.
$\begin{align*}C &= \pi d\\C &= \pi\times6\\C &\approx 18.850\text{ cm}\end{align*}$

The marked length is the radius.
$\begin{align*}C &= 2\pi r\\C &= 2\times\pi\times3.2\\C &\approx 20.106\text{ m}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text:
Find the exact circumference of each circle in terms of $\pi$.
a. Diameter $16$ cm.
b. Radius $4$ m.
workedExamples.solution_text:
a.
$\begin{align*}C &= \pi d\\C &= \pi\times16\\C &= 16\pi\text{ cm}\end{align*}$
b.
$\begin{align*}C &= 2\pi r\\C &= 2\times\pi\times4\\C &= 8\pi\text{ m}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: Circle A has radius $18$ mm. Circle B has diameter $4.2$ cm. Find both circumferences in millimetres, correct to 2 decimal places, and identify the larger circumference. Express Circle A’s circumference as a fraction of Circle B’s circumference. Give the fraction exactly.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Circle A:
$\begin{align*}C_A &= 2\pi r\\C_A &= 2\times\pi\times18\\C_A &= 36\pi\text{ mm}\\C_A &\approx 113.10\text{ mm}\end{align*}$
Circle B has diameter $4.2\text{ cm}=42\text{ mm}$.
$\begin{align*}C_B &= \pi d\\C_B &= \pi\times42\\C_B &= 42\pi\text{ mm}\\C_B &\approx 131.95\text{ mm}\end{align*}$
Circle B has the larger circumference. Divide the exact circumferences to compare them.
$\begin{align*}\frac{C_A}{C_B} &= \frac{36\pi}{42\pi}\\\frac{C_A}{C_B} &= \frac{6}{7}\end{align*}$
Circle A's circumference is $\frac{6}{7}$ times Circle B's circumference.

workedExamples.question_text: Circle P has radius $8$ m. Circle Q has diameter $16$ m. Find their exact circumferences and explain what the answers show.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Circle P:
$\begin{align*}C_P &= 2\pi r\\C_P &= 2\times\pi\times8\\C_P &= 16\pi\text{ m}\end{align*}$
Circle Q:
$\begin{align*}C_Q &= \pi d\\C_Q &= \pi\times16\\C_Q &= 16\pi\text{ m}\end{align*}$
Both circles have diameter $16$ m, so they have the same size and circumference.

workedExamples.question_text: A circle has diameter $7$ cm. A student writes $C=2\times\pi\times7\approx43.98\text{ cm}$. Explain the mistake and find the correct circumference to 2 decimal places.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The student used the diameter as the radius. Use $C=\pi d$ for the given diameter.
$\begin{align*}C &= \pi d\\C &= \pi\times7\\C &\approx 21.99\text{ cm}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: An athlete jogs $6$ laps of a circular track with radius $35$ m. How far does the athlete jog? Round to the nearest metre.
workedExamples.solution_text:
One lap is the circumference.
$\begin{align*}C &= 2\pi r\\C &= 2\times\pi\times35\\C &= 70\pi\text{ m}\\\text{Distance} &= 6\times70\pi\\\text{Distance} &\approx 1319\text{ m}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A bicycle wheel has diameter $480$ mm and turns $4$ times. How far does the bicycle travel, in metres, correct to 2 decimal places?
workedExamples.solution_text:
Each revolution moves the bicycle forward by one circumference.
$\begin{align*}C &= \pi d\\C &= \pi\times480\\C &= 480\pi\text{ mm}\\\text{Distance} &= 4\times480\pi\\\text{Distance} &= 1920\pi\text{ mm}\\\text{Distance in metres} &= \frac{1920\pi}{1000}\\\text{Distance in metres} &\approx 6.03\text{ m}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A cyclist travels $5$ km on a bicycle whose wheels have diameter $60$ cm. How many revolutions does each wheel make? Round to the nearest whole number.
workedExamples.solution_text:
One revolution covers one circumference.
$\begin{align*}C &= \pi d\\C &= \pi\times60\\C &= 60\pi\text{ cm}\end{align*}$
$5\text{ km}=500\,000\text{ cm}$.
$\begin{align*}\text{Revolutions} &= \frac{500\,000}{60\pi}\\\text{Revolutions} &= 2652.582\ldots\\\text{Revolutions} &\approx 2653\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A Ferris wheel has diameter $70$ m. Its pods must be spaced at least $9$ m apart around the circumference. Each pod carries $8$ passengers. What is the greatest number of passengers the wheel can carry at one time?
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}C &= \pi d\\C &= \pi\times70\\C &= 70\pi\text{ m}\\\frac{C}{9} &= \frac{70\pi}{9}\\\frac{C}{9} &= 24.434\ldots\end{align*}$
At most $24$ pods fit; $25$ pods would require $225$ m, which exceeds the circumference.
$\text{Passengers}=24\times8=192$.

workedExamples.question_text: An object follows a circular orbit of radius $240\,000$ km and completes one orbit in $20$ days. How many kilometres does it travel each hour? Round to the nearest whole number.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}C &= 2\pi r\\C &= 2\times\pi\times240\,000\\C &= 480\,000\pi\text{ km}\end{align*}$
The orbit takes $20\times24=480$ hours.
$\begin{align*}\text{Distance per hour} &= \frac{480\,000\pi}{480}\\\text{Distance per hour} &= 1000\pi\\\text{Distance per hour} &\approx 3142\text{ km/h}\end{align*}$

development.question_text: A circular water tank has a diameter of $3.5$ m. Find the distance around the tank, correct to $1$ decimal place.

An athlete trains on a circular track of radius $40$ m and jogs $10$ laps.
How far does the athlete jog, to the nearest metre?

A bicycle wheel has a diameter of $530$ mm.
The wheel turns $3$ times.
How far does the bicycle travel, in metres, correct to $1$ decimal place?
A circular garden bed has a radius of $12$ m. Find the length of edging needed to go around it, in exact form in terms of $\pi$.

development.solution_text:
Sushi A: $C = 2\pi r$
$= 2 \times \pi \times 20$
$\approx 125.66\text{ mm}$
Sushi B: $4.5\text{ cm} = 45\text{ mm}$
$C = \pi d$
$= \pi \times 45$
$\approx 141.37\text{ mm}$
Sushi B has the larger circumference.

Circle P: $C = 2\pi r$
$= 2 \times \pi \times 9$
$= 18\pi\text{ m}$
Circle Q: $C = \pi d$
$= \pi \times 18$
$= 18\pi\text{ m}$
A radius of $9$ m gives a diameter of $18$ m, so P and Q are the same circle described in two ways.

Circle A: $C = \pi d$
$= \pi \times 6$
$= 6\pi\text{ cm}$
Circle B: $C = \pi d$
$= \pi \times 12$
$= 12\pi\text{ cm}$
$12\pi \div 6\pi = 2$, so circle B's circumference is twice circle A's.

The $5$ cm marked is the diameter, not the radius, so $C = \pi d$ should be used.
$C = \pi d$
$= \pi \times 5$
$\approx 15.71\text{ cm}$

mastery.question_text:
A Ferris wheel has a diameter of $80$ m. Its pods each carry $10$ passengers and must be spaced at least $10$ m apart around the circumference.
What is the greatest number of passengers that can be on the Ferris wheel at one time?
mastery.solution_text:
$C = \pi d$
$= \pi \times 80$
$= 251.3274\ldots\text{ m}$
$251.3274\ldots \div 10 = 25.13\ldots$, so at most $25$ pods fit
$25 \times 10 = 250$ passengers

mastery.question_text:
Faith goes on a $12$ km bike ride.
Each wheel of her bike has a diameter of $55$ cm.
How many revolutions does a wheel make during the ride?
Round to the nearest whole number.

The Moon travels around the Earth on a path very close to a circle of radius $384\,400$ km, and takes $27.32$ days to complete one orbit.
How many kilometres does the Moon travel each hour?
Round to the nearest whole number.
